explanations.answer: A house for the ark of the covenant
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. David says it was in his heart to build a house as a resting place for the ark of the covenant of the LORD and as a footstool for our God. He wasn't just daydreaming over coffee, either. He tells the crowd he'd already gotten ready to build it.

explanations.answer: A palace of cedar for himself
explanations.explanation: I see why you went there, because David did live in a house of cedar (2 Samuel 7:2). But the dream he shares in this speech isn't about his own place. He says it was in his heart to build a resting place for the ark of the covenant of the LORD. Nothing in it is about David's own comfort.

explanations.answer: A wall around all of Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: David never brings up a wall in this speech. He says it was in his heart to build a house as a resting place for the ark of the covenant of the LORD and a footstool for our God. Jerusalem will have to find another contractor for its wall, friend.

True! David says, “I had made preparations to build it,” so the plans were already moving. This king didn't just say 'someday.' He had his apron on and the oven warm. I think that makes the next part even harder to hear.

Close, but David says the opposite. In verse 2 he says, “I had made preparations to build it,” so he'd already started getting ready. He wasn't just wishing, friend. He was working on it before God ever said a word about who would build.

explanations.answer: He is a man of war who shed blood
explanations.explanation: Yes. David tells the crowd God said, “You are not to build a house for My Name, because you are a man of war who has shed blood.” That's a heavy thing to say out loud in front of everybody. I think it took real humility for David to repeat it to the whole room.

explanations.answer: He is too old to see it finished
explanations.explanation: Age never comes up in what God says. The reason David gives is that he is a man of war who has shed blood. God said, “You are not to build a house for My Name, because you are a man of war who has shed blood.” You'd think a reason like that would have a wrinkle or two in it, but no.

explanations.answer: He did not ask the priests first
explanations.explanation: The priests don't show up in this part of the speech at all. David says God spoke to him directly: “You are not to build a house for My Name, because you are a man of war who has shed blood.” So the reason came straight from God, not from a meeting with the priests.

Right on target. David says, “He chose Judah as leader,” and then he zooms in. From the house of Judah God chose his father's household, and from his father's sons God was pleased to make him king over all Israel. It's like a map app, friend: tribe, then household, then one king in the middle of it all.

Benjamin is a real tribe of Israel, and Saul, Israel's first king, came from it (1 Samuel 9:1-2). But David says God chose Judah as leader. From the house of Judah, God chose his father's household, and from there, David himself.

Levi's people do show up later in this speech, serving in the house of the LORD. But David doesn't name Levi as the tribe chosen as leader. He says, “He chose Judah as leader,” and then walks down from there to his own father's household.

That's him. Solomon, David's son, is the one David says the LORD has chosen to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel. David says the LORD has given him many sons, and still the choice is one. Many sons, one throne.

Absalom was one of David's sons (2 Samuel 3:3), so I see where you were headed. But the one David names in this speech is Solomon. He says, “He has chosen Solomon my son to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel.”

Adonijah was another of David's sons (2 Samuel 3:4), so it was a fair guess from the family. But the name David speaks to the whole assembly is Solomon. David says the LORD chose Solomon out of all his sons to sit on the throne.

Yes, son. God says of Solomon, “…for I have chosen him as My son…” That's not a small word to hear from the One who made everything, friend. David is repeating it right there in front of the whole room.
Yes, Father. God says of Solomon, “…and I will be his Father.” David passes along the words just as he heard them.
Servant is a word that gets used a lot in the Bible, but it isn't the one God uses for Solomon here. He says, “…for I have chosen him as My son…” So the word he picks is son.
Shepherd isn't the word God uses in this verse. God says of Solomon, “…and I will be his Father.” He calls Himself Solomon's Father, so that's the one that fits the blank.
Judge doesn't show up anywhere in this part of the speech. What God says is, “…for I have chosen him as My son, and I will be his Father.” So the blanks are son and Father.

explanations.answer: He resolutely carries out God's commandments
explanations.explanation: That's the condition. God says, “I will establish his kingdom forever, if he resolutely carries out My commandments and ordinances…” The word is resolutely, friend. That means no halfway and no 'I'll get to it Thursday.'

explanations.answer: He finishes building the house quickly
explanations.explanation: God doesn't put a speed limit on Solomon. The condition is that he resolutely carries out God's commandments and ordinances. God says, “I will establish his kingdom forever, if he resolutely carries out My commandments and ordinances…” Nobody is holding a stopwatch over the oven here.

explanations.answer: He defeats every enemy around Israel
explanations.explanation: Enemies don't come up in this promise at all. God says, “I will establish his kingdom forever, if he resolutely carries out My commandments and ordinances…” The condition is about following God's commands. Beating every enemy isn't on that list.

explanations.answer: They possess the good land and pass it down
explanations.explanation: You've got it. David says to keep and seek out all the commandments of the LORD your God, “so that you may possess this good land and leave it as an inheritance to your descendants forever.” So it's about the land now and the family later. The people in that room would pass it on.

explanations.answer: They never have to face another war
explanations.explanation: David doesn't promise a war-free future. He says the reason to keep and seek out the commandments is “so that you may possess this good land and leave it as an inheritance to your descendants forever.” That's the promise on the table.

explanations.answer: Their storehouses stay full every single year
explanations.explanation: That would be nice, friend, but David never says it. He says to keep and seek out all the commandments “so that you may possess this good land and leave it as an inheritance to your descendants forever.” The promise is about the land and passing it down.

Yes. David tells Solomon to serve with a willing mind “for the LORD searches every heart and understands the intent of every thought.” That's a lot of searching, friend. You can't hand God a cookie that only looks good on top.

David never says anything about enemies watching Solomon. His reason is, “…for the LORD searches every heart and understands the intent of every thought.” The One who matters is already looking at the heart.

explanations.answer: The prophets judge all his work
explanations.explanation: Prophets don't come up in this part of David's charge. The reason he gives is, “…for the LORD searches every heart and understands the intent of every thought.” So the focus is on the heart before God.
True! David tells Solomon, “If you seek Him, He will be found by you…” That's a promise worth keeping close. Seek, and He will be found.
David actually says the opposite of false here. He tells Solomon, “If you seek Him, He will be found by you…” So when Solomon seeks the LORD, he can count on finding Him.

David says the opposite here, and it's a serious line. He tells Solomon, “…if you forsake Him, He will reject you forever.” So the statement that the LORD would never reject him doesn't match what David says.

False is right. David tells Solomon, “…if you forsake Him, He will reject you forever.” It sits right next to the promise that seeking Him means finding Him. It's a heavy line, so I think David wanted Solomon to hear it plainly.

explanations.answer: The LORD made them clear to him in writing
explanations.explanation: That's it. David says, “…the LORD has made clear to me in writing by His hand upon me.” So the plan didn't come from David's own sketch pad. Every detail was made clear to him by the LORD.

explanations.answer: His counselors drew them up over many years
explanations.explanation: David never mentions counselors drawing anything up. He says, “…the LORD has made clear to me in writing by His hand upon me.” The source is the LORD, not a committee.

explanations.answer: He copied them from the old tabernacle plans
explanations.explanation: David doesn't mention tabernacle plans at all. He says, “…the LORD has made clear to me in writing by His hand upon me.” So the details came from the LORD, and I'd say that beats any copy of a copy.

True! David tells Solomon, “Do not be afraid or discouraged, for the LORD God, my God, is with you.” Notice that David says my God. He's handing his son the biggest job of his life, and he's telling him he won't be doing it alone.

David says exactly that. He tells Solomon, “Do not be afraid or discouraged, for the LORD God, my God, is with you.” So the statement is true, and the reason for Solomon not to be afraid is that the LORD God is with him.

House is the word. David says the LORD will neither fail nor forsake Solomon “…before all the work for the service of the house of the LORD is finished.” So the promise lasts all the way to the last bit of work. He doesn't leave before the oven is turned off.

City sounds close, but it isn't the word David uses. He says the LORD will not fail or forsake Solomon “…before all the work for the service of the house of the LORD is finished.” The work is about the house of the LORD.

The people do show up in David's speech, but not in this promise. He says the LORD will neither fail nor forsake Solomon “…before all the work for the service of the house of the LORD is finished.” The word that fits the blank is house.

explanations.answer: Every willing man of every skill
explanations.explanation: Yes. David says, “…every willing man of every skill will be at your disposal for the work.” Willing and skilled, friend. That's the kind of crew you want in any kitchen.

explanations.answer: Only the strongest men of Judah
explanations.explanation: David doesn't limit it to the strongest men or to Judah. He says, “…every willing man of every skill will be at your disposal for the work.” So all kinds of skills are welcome, not just muscle.

explanations.answer: Workers paid from the royal treasury
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say anything about how these workers are paid. What he says is, “…every willing man of every skill will be at your disposal for the work.” The word that stands out is willing.
